mn101:1.2: On one occasion the Blessed One was living among the Sakyans, at a town of the Sakyans called Devadaha.
mn101:1.3: There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
mn101:2.2: “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
mn101:2.4: “Bhikkhus, there are some ascetics and brahmins who have this doctrine and this view:
mn101:2.5: ‘Whatever this person experiences, whether pleasure, or pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure, all that is caused by what was done in the past.[^1]
mn101:2.6: So, by annihilating past deeds through austerity, and by doing no new deeds, there is no consequence for the future;
mn101:2.7: with no consequence for the future, there is the exhaustion of deeds; with the exhaustion of deeds, there is the exhaustion of suffering; with the exhaustion of suffering, there is the exhaustion of feeling; with the exhaustion of feeling, all suffering will be worn away.’
mn101:2.8: This, bhikkhus, is the doctrine of the Nigaṇṭhas.
mn101:3.1: Having this doctrine, bhikkhus, I went to the Nigaṇṭhas and said:
mn101:3.2: ‘Is it true, friend Nigaṇṭhas, as they say, that you have this doctrine and this view—
mn101:3.3: “whatever this person experiences, whether pleasure, or pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure, all that is caused by what was done in the past.
mn101:3.4: So, by annihilating past deeds through austerity, and by doing no new deeds, there is no consequence for the future;
mn101:3.5: with no consequence for the future, there is the exhaustion of deeds; with the exhaustion of deeds, there is the exhaustion of suffering; with the exhaustion of suffering, there is the exhaustion of feeling; with the exhaustion of feeling, all suffering will be worn away”?’
mn101:3.6: And those Nigaṇṭhas, bhikkhus, being asked thus, admitted it, saying: ‘Yes.’
mn101:4.3: “we existed in the past, we did not not exist”?’[^2]
mn101:4.6: “we did evil deeds in the past, we did not not do them”?’
mn101:4.12: “so much suffering has been worn away, or so much suffering has yet to be worn away, or when so much suffering has been worn away, all suffering will have been worn away”?’
mn101:4.15: “the abandoning of unwholesome things and the achievement of wholesome things here and now”?’
mn101:5.1: ‘So then, friend Nigaṇṭhas, it seems you do not know—
mn101:5.2: “we existed in the past, we did not not exist”; you do not know—
mn101:5.3: “we did evil deeds in the past, we did not not do them”; you do not know—
mn101:5.4: “we did such-and-such an evil deed”; you do not know—
mn101:5.5: “so much suffering has been worn away, or so much suffering has yet to be worn away, or when so much suffering has been worn away, all suffering will have been worn away”; you do not know—
mn101:5.6: the abandoning of unwholesome things and the achievement of wholesome things here and now;
mn101:5.7: that being so, it is not fitting for the venerable Nigaṇṭhas to declare:
mn101:5.8: “whatever this person experiences, whether pleasure, or pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure, all that is caused by what was done in the past.
mn101:5.9: So, by annihilating past deeds through austerity, and by doing no new deeds, there is no consequence for the future;
mn101:5.10: with no consequence for the future, there is the exhaustion of deeds; with the exhaustion of deeds, there is the exhaustion of suffering; with the exhaustion of suffering, there is the exhaustion of feeling; with the exhaustion of feeling, all suffering will be worn away.”’
mn101:6.2: “we existed in the past, we did not not exist”; if you knew—
mn101:6.3: “we did evil deeds in the past, we did not not do them”; if you knew—
mn101:6.4: “we did such-and-such an evil deed”; if you knew—
mn101:6.5: “so much suffering has been worn away, or so much suffering has yet to be worn away, or when so much suffering has been worn away, all suffering will have been worn away”; if you knew—
mn101:6.6: the abandoning of unwholesome things and the achievement of wholesome things here and now;
mn101:6.7: that being so, it would be fitting for the venerable Nigaṇṭhas to declare:

mn101:6.9: So, by annihilating past deeds through austerity, and by doing no new deeds, there is no consequence for the future;
mn101:6.10: with no consequence for the future, there is the exhaustion of deeds; with the exhaustion of deeds, there is the exhaustion of suffering; with the exhaustion of suffering, there is the exhaustion of feeling; with the exhaustion of feeling, all suffering will be worn away.”’
mn101:7.1: ‘Suppose, friend Nigaṇṭhas, a man were wounded by an arrow thickly smeared with poison;
mn101:7.2: because of the arrow’s piercing, he would feel painful, sharp, severe feelings.
mn101:7.3: His friends and companions, his relatives and kin, would bring a surgeon to treat him.
mn101:7.4: The surgeon would cut round the opening of the wound with a knife;
mn101:7.5: because of the knife’s cutting round the opening of the wound, he would feel painful, sharp, severe feelings.
mn101:7.6: The surgeon would probe for the arrow with a probe;
mn101:7.7: because of the probe’s probing for the arrow, he would feel painful, sharp, severe feelings.
mn101:7.8: The surgeon would pull out the arrow;
mn101:7.9: because of the pulling out of the arrow, he would feel painful, sharp, severe feelings.
mn101:7.10: The surgeon would apply a caustic medicine to the opening of the wound;
mn101:7.11: because of the caustic medicine applied to the opening of the wound, he would feel painful, sharp, severe feelings.
mn101:7.12: On a later occasion, with the wound healed and covered with skin, he would be well, happy, independent, his own master, able to go where he likes.
mn101:7.14: “Formerly I was wounded by an arrow thickly smeared with poison.
mn101:7.15: Because of the arrow’s piercing, I felt painful, sharp, severe feelings.
mn101:7.16: My friends and companions, my relatives and kin, brought a surgeon to treat me.
mn101:7.17: The surgeon cut round the opening of the wound with a knife;
mn101:7.18: because of the knife’s cutting round the opening of the wound, I felt painful, sharp, severe feelings.
mn101:7.19: The surgeon probed for the arrow with a probe;
mn101:7.20: because of the probe’s probing for the arrow, I felt painful, sharp, severe feelings.
mn101:7.21: The surgeon pulled out the arrow;[^4]
mn101:7.22: because of the pulling out of the arrow, I felt painful, sharp, severe feelings.
mn101:7.23: The surgeon applied a caustic medicine to the opening of the wound;
mn101:7.24: because of the caustic medicine applied to the opening of the wound, I felt painful, sharp, severe feelings.
mn101:7.25: Now, with the wound healed and covered with skin, I am well, happy, independent, my own master, able to go where I like.”’
mn101:8.1: ‘So too, friend Nigaṇṭhas, if you knew—
mn101:8.2: “we existed in the past, we did not not exist”; if you knew—
mn101:8.3: “we did evil deeds in the past, we did not not do them”; if you knew—
mn101:8.4: “we did such-and-such an evil deed”; if you knew—
mn101:8.5: “so much suffering has been worn away, or so much suffering has yet to be worn away, or when so much suffering has been worn away, all suffering will have been worn away”; if you knew—
mn101:8.6: the abandoning of unwholesome things and the achievement of wholesome things here and now;
mn101:8.7: that being so, it would be fitting for the venerable Nigaṇṭhas to declare:
mn101:8.8: “whatever this person experiences, whether pleasure, or pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure, all that is caused by what was done in the past.
mn101:8.9: So, by annihilating past deeds through austerity, and by doing no new deeds, there is no consequence for the future;
mn101:8.10: with no consequence for the future, there is the exhaustion of deeds; with the exhaustion of deeds, there is the exhaustion of suffering; with the exhaustion of suffering, there is the exhaustion of feeling; with the exhaustion of feeling, all suffering will be worn away.”’
mn101:9.1: ‘But since, friend Nigaṇṭhas, you do not know—
mn101:9.2: “we existed in the past, we did not not exist”; you do not know—
mn101:9.3: “we did evil deeds in the past, we did not not do them”; you do not know—
mn101:9.4: “we did such-and-such an evil deed”; you do not know—
mn101:9.5: “so much suffering has been worn away, or so much suffering has yet to be worn away, or when so much suffering has been worn away, all suffering will have been worn away”; you do not know—
mn101:9.6: the abandoning of unwholesome things and the achievement of wholesome things here and now;
mn101:9.7: therefore it is not fitting for the venerable Nigaṇṭhas to declare:
mn101:9.8: “whatever this person experiences, whether pleasure, or pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure, all that is caused by what was done in the past.
mn101:9.9: So, by annihilating past deeds through austerity, and by doing no new deeds, there is no consequence for the future;
mn101:9.10: with no consequence for the future, there is the exhaustion of deeds; with the exhaustion of deeds, there is the exhaustion of suffering; with the exhaustion of suffering, there is the exhaustion of feeling; with the exhaustion of feeling, all suffering will be worn away.”’
mn101:10.1: When this was said, bhikkhus, those Nigaṇṭhas said to me:
mn101:10.2: ‘Friend, the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta is omniscient and all-seeing, and claims to have complete knowledge and vision thus:
mn101:10.3: “whether I am walking or standing, asleep or awake, knowledge and vision are continuously and unceasingly present to me.”
mn101:10.5: “Nigaṇṭhas, you have done evil deeds in the past; wear them away by this severe austerity;[^5]
mn101:10.6: and as to being restrained here and now in body, speech, and mind, that is the non-doing of evil deeds for the future.
mn101:10.7: So, by annihilating past deeds through austerity, and by doing no new deeds, there is no consequence for the future;
mn101:10.8: with no consequence for the future, there is the exhaustion of deeds; with the exhaustion of deeds, there is the exhaustion of suffering; with the exhaustion of suffering, there is the exhaustion of feeling; with the exhaustion of feeling, all suffering will be worn away.”
mn101:10.9: And this is to our liking and satisfaction, and so we are pleased.’
mn101:11.1: When this was said, bhikkhus, I said to those Nigaṇṭhas:
mn101:11.2: ‘There are, friend Nigaṇṭhas, these five things which have a twofold result in this very life.
mn101:11.4: Faith, liking, oral tradition, reasoned reflection, and acceptance of a view after pondering it[^6]—
mn101:11.5: these, friend Nigaṇṭhas, are the five things which have a twofold result in this very life.
mn101:11.6: Now, as regards your teacher’s teaching about the past, what is the venerable Nigaṇṭhas’ faith, what is their liking, what is their oral tradition, what is their reasoned reflection, what is their acceptance of a view after pondering it?’
mn101:11.7: Speaking thus, bhikkhus, I do not see any legitimate rebuttal from the Nigaṇṭhas.
mn101:12.1: Again, bhikkhus, I said to those Nigaṇṭhas:
mn101:12.3: On the occasion when there is intense exertion, intense striving, do you on that occasion feel painful, sharp, severe feelings caused by that exertion;
mn101:12.4: and on the occasion when there is no intense exertion, no intense striving, do you on that occasion not feel painful, sharp, severe feelings caused by that exertion?’
mn101:12.5: ‘On the occasion, friend Gotama, when there is intense exertion, intense striving, we feel painful, sharp, severe feelings caused by that exertion;
mn101:12.6: and on the occasion when there is no intense exertion, no intense striving, we do not feel painful, sharp, severe feelings caused by that exertion.’
mn101:13.1: ‘So then, friend Nigaṇṭhas, it seems that on the occasion when there is intense exertion, intense striving, you feel painful, sharp, severe feelings caused by that exertion;[^7]
mn101:13.2: and on the occasion when there is no intense exertion, no intense striving, you do not feel painful, sharp, severe feelings caused by that exertion.
mn101:13.3: That being so, it is not fitting for the venerable Nigaṇṭhas to declare:
mn101:13.4: “whatever this person experiences, whether pleasure, or pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure, all that is caused by what was done in the past.
mn101:13.5: So, by annihilating past deeds through austerity, and by doing no new deeds, there is no consequence for the future;
mn101:13.6: with no consequence for the future, there is the exhaustion of deeds; with the exhaustion of deeds, there is the exhaustion of suffering; with the exhaustion of suffering, there is the exhaustion of feeling; with the exhaustion of feeling, all suffering will be worn away.”’
mn101:14.1: ‘If, friend Nigaṇṭhas, on the occasion when there is intense exertion, intense striving, you were not to feel painful, sharp, severe feelings caused by that exertion;
mn101:14.2: and on the occasion when there is no intense exertion, no intense striving, you were to feel painful, sharp, severe feelings caused by that exertion;
mn101:14.3: that being so, it would be fitting for the venerable Nigaṇṭhas to declare:
mn101:14.4: “whatever this person experiences, whether pleasure, or pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure, all that is caused by what was done in the past.
mn101:14.5: So, by annihilating past deeds through austerity, and by doing no new deeds, there is no consequence for the future;
mn101:14.6: with no consequence for the future, there is the exhaustion of deeds; with the exhaustion of deeds, there is the exhaustion of suffering; with the exhaustion of suffering, there is the exhaustion of feeling; with the exhaustion of feeling, all suffering will be worn away.”’
mn101:15.1: ‘But since, friend Nigaṇṭhas, on the occasion when there is intense exertion, intense striving, you feel painful, sharp, severe feelings caused by that exertion;
mn101:15.2: and on the occasion when there is no intense exertion, no intense striving, you do not feel painful, sharp, severe feelings caused by that exertion;
mn101:15.3: you yourselves, feeling painful, sharp, severe feelings due to that self-imposed exertion, mistakenly believe, through ignorance, unknowing, and delusion:
mn101:15.4: “whatever this person experiences, whether pleasure, or pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure, all that is caused by what was done in the past.
mn101:15.5: So, by annihilating past deeds through austerity, and by doing no new deeds, there is no consequence for the future;
mn101:15.6: with no consequence for the future, there is the exhaustion of deeds; with the exhaustion of deeds, there is the exhaustion of suffering; with the exhaustion of suffering, there is the exhaustion of feeling; with the exhaustion of feeling, all suffering will be worn away.”’
mn101:15.7: Speaking thus too, bhikkhus, I do not see any legitimate rebuttal from the Nigaṇṭhas.
mn101:16.1: Again, bhikkhus, I said to those Nigaṇṭhas:
mn101:16.2: ‘What do you think, friend Nigaṇṭhas: is it possible that a deed to be experienced here and now could, by exertion or striving, become a deed to be experienced in a future life?’
mn101:16.4: ‘But is it possible that a deed to be experienced in a future life could, by exertion or striving, become a deed to be experienced here and now?’
mn101:17.1: ‘What do you think, friend Nigaṇṭhas: is it possible that a deed to be experienced as pleasure could, by exertion or striving, become a deed to be experienced as pain?’
mn101:17.3: ‘But is it possible that a deed to be experienced as pain could, by exertion or striving, become a deed to be experienced as pleasure?’
mn101:18.1: ‘What do you think, friend Nigaṇṭhas: is it possible that a deed to be experienced when mature could, by exertion or striving, become a deed to be experienced when immature?’[^8]
mn101:18.3: ‘But is it possible that a deed to be experienced when immature could, by exertion or striving, become a deed to be experienced when mature?’
mn101:19.1: ‘What do you think, friend Nigaṇṭhas: is it possible that a deed to be experienced much could, by exertion or striving, become a deed to be experienced little?’
mn101:19.3: ‘But is it possible that a deed to be experienced little could, by exertion or striving, become a deed to be experienced much?’
mn101:20.1: ‘What do you think, friend Nigaṇṭhas: is it possible that a deed to be experienced could, by exertion or striving, become a deed not to be experienced?’
mn101:20.3: ‘But is it possible that a deed not to be experienced could, by exertion or striving, become a deed to be experienced?’
mn101:21.1: ‘So then, friend Nigaṇṭhas, it seems it is not possible that a deed to be experienced here and now could, by exertion or striving, become a deed to be experienced in a future life; it is not possible that a deed to be experienced in a future life could, by exertion or striving, become a deed to be experienced here and now; it is not possible that a deed to be experienced as pleasure could, by exertion or striving, become a deed to be experienced as pain; it is not possible that a deed to be experienced as pain could, by exertion or striving, become a deed to be experienced as pleasure; it is not possible that a deed to be experienced when mature could, by exertion or striving, become a deed to be experienced when immature; it is not possible that a deed to be experienced when immature could, by exertion or striving, become a deed to be experienced when mature; it is not possible that a deed to be experienced much could, by exertion or striving, become a deed to be experienced little; it is not possible that a deed to be experienced little could, by exertion or striving, become a deed to be experienced much; it is not possible that a deed to be experienced could, by exertion or striving, become a deed not to be experienced; it is not possible that a deed not to be experienced could, by exertion or striving, become a deed to be experienced;
mn101:21.2: that being so, the venerable Nigaṇṭhas’ exertion is fruitless, their striving is fruitless.’
mn101:22.1: This, bhikkhus, is the doctrine of the Nigaṇṭhas.
mn101:22.2: For the Nigaṇṭhas who hold this doctrine, bhikkhus, there are ten legitimate deductions that give ground for censure.
mn101:22.3: If, bhikkhus, beings experience pleasure and pain because of what was done in the past,
mn101:22.4: then surely, bhikkhus, the Nigaṇṭhas were doers of evil deeds in the past, since they now feel such painful, sharp, severe feelings.
mn101:22.5: If, bhikkhus, beings experience pleasure and pain because of creation by a supreme god,
mn101:22.6: then surely, bhikkhus, the Nigaṇṭhas were created by an evil supreme god, since they now feel such painful, sharp, severe feelings.
mn101:22.7: If, bhikkhus, beings experience pleasure and pain because of circumstance,[^9]
mn101:22.8: then surely, bhikkhus, the Nigaṇṭhas have bad circumstances, since they now feel such painful, sharp, severe feelings.
mn101:22.9: If, bhikkhus, beings experience pleasure and pain because of class of origin,[^10]
mn101:22.10: then surely, bhikkhus, the Nigaṇṭhas have a bad class of origin, since they now feel such painful, sharp, severe feelings.
mn101:22.11: If, bhikkhus, beings experience pleasure and pain because of present exertion,
mn101:22.12: then surely, bhikkhus, the Nigaṇṭhas have made bad present exertion, since they now feel such painful, sharp, severe feelings.
mn101:22.13: If, bhikkhus, beings experience pleasure and pain because of what was done in the past, the Nigaṇṭhas are to be blamed;
mn101:22.14: if beings do not experience pleasure and pain because of what was done in the past, the Nigaṇṭhas are to be blamed.
mn101:22.15: If, bhikkhus, beings experience pleasure and pain because of creation by a supreme god, the Nigaṇṭhas are to be blamed;
mn101:22.16: if beings do not experience pleasure and pain because of creation by a supreme god, the Nigaṇṭhas are to be blamed.
mn101:22.17: If, bhikkhus, beings experience pleasure and pain because of circumstance, the Nigaṇṭhas are to be blamed;
mn101:22.18: if beings do not experience pleasure and pain because of circumstance, the Nigaṇṭhas are to be blamed.
mn101:22.19: If, bhikkhus, beings experience pleasure and pain because of class of origin, the Nigaṇṭhas are to be blamed;
mn101:22.20: if beings do not experience pleasure and pain because of class of origin, the Nigaṇṭhas are to be blamed.
mn101:22.21: If, bhikkhus, beings experience pleasure and pain because of present exertion, the Nigaṇṭhas are to be blamed;
mn101:22.22: if beings do not experience pleasure and pain because of present exertion, the Nigaṇṭhas are to be blamed.
mn101:22.23: This, bhikkhus, is the doctrine of the Nigaṇṭhas.
mn101:22.24: For the Nigaṇṭhas who hold this doctrine, bhikkhus, these ten legitimate deductions give ground for censure.
mn101:22.25: So, bhikkhus, exertion is fruitless in this way, striving is fruitless in this way.
mn101:23.1: And how, bhikkhus, is exertion fruitful, how is striving fruitful?
mn101:23.2: Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who is not yet free from suffering does not add further suffering to himself,[^11] nor does he give up pleasure that accords with the Dhamma, yet he is not infatuated with that pleasure.
mn101:23.4: ‘When I strive with active effort against this source of suffering, then, through that active effort, there comes to be fading away of this source; but when I look on with equanimity at this source of suffering, then, while developing equanimity, there comes to be fading away of this source.’
mn101:23.5: So he strives with active effort against that source of suffering for which, through active effort, there comes to be fading away;
mn101:23.6: and he develops equanimity in regard to that source of suffering for which, while developing equanimity, there comes to be fading away.
mn101:23.7: For that source of suffering for which, through active effort, there comes to be fading away, by striving with active effort—
mn101:23.8: in that way that suffering is worn away in him.
mn101:23.9: And for that source of suffering for which, while developing equanimity, there comes to be fading away, by developing equanimity—
mn101:23.10: in that way too that suffering is worn away in him.
mn101:24.1: Suppose, bhikkhus, a man were enamoured of a woman, with his mind bound to her, with intense desire, intense longing.
mn101:24.2: He might see that woman standing with another man, chatting, laughing, and joking together.
mn101:24.4: would sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise in that man on seeing that woman standing with another man, chatting, laughing, and joking together?”
mn101:24.7: “Because, venerable sir, that man is enamoured of that woman, with his mind bound to her, with intense desire, intense longing;
mn101:24.8: that is why, on seeing that woman standing with another man, chatting, laughing, and joking together, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair would arise in him.”
mn101:25.1: “Then, bhikkhus, it might occur to that man:
mn101:25.2: ‘I am enamoured of that woman, with my mind bound to her, with intense desire, intense longing.
mn101:25.3: On seeing that woman standing with another man, chatting, laughing, and joking together, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise in me.
mn101:25.4: Suppose I were to abandon the desire and lust I have for that woman?’
mn101:25.5: So he abandons the desire and lust he has for that woman.
mn101:25.6: Then, on a later occasion, he might see that woman standing with another man, chatting, laughing, and joking together.
mn101:25.8: would sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise in that man on seeing that woman standing with another man, chatting, laughing, and joking together?”
mn101:25.11: “Because, venerable sir, that man is without lust for that woman.
mn101:25.12: That is why, on seeing that woman standing with another man, chatting, laughing, and joking together, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair would not arise in him.”
mn101:26.1: “So too, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who is not yet free from suffering does not add further suffering to himself, nor does he give up pleasure that accords with the Dhamma, yet he is not infatuated with that pleasure.
mn101:26.3: ‘When I strive with active effort against this source of suffering, then, through that active effort, there comes to be fading away of this source; but when I look on with equanimity at this source of suffering, then, while developing equanimity, there comes to be fading away of this source.’
mn101:26.4: So he strives with active effort against that source of suffering for which, through active effort, there comes to be fading away;
mn101:26.5: and he develops equanimity in regard to that source of suffering for which, while developing equanimity, there comes to be fading away.
mn101:26.6: For that source of suffering for which, through active effort, there comes to be fading away, by striving with active effort—
mn101:26.7: in that way that suffering is worn away in him.
mn101:26.8: And for that source of suffering for which, while developing equanimity, there comes to be fading away, by developing equanimity—
mn101:26.9: in that way too that suffering is worn away in him.
mn101:26.10: In this way too, bhikkhus, exertion is fruitful, striving is fruitful.
mn101:27.1: Again, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu considers thus:
mn101:27.2: ‘When I dwell at ease, unwholesome things increase in me and wholesome things decline;
mn101:27.3: but when I apply myself to painful striving, unwholesome things decline in me and wholesome things increase.
mn101:27.4: Suppose I were to apply myself to painful striving?’[^12]
mn101:27.5: So he applies himself to painful striving.
mn101:27.6: When he applies himself to painful striving, unwholesome things decline in him and wholesome things increase.
mn101:27.7: On a later occasion he does not apply himself to painful striving again.
mn101:27.9: Because, bhikkhus, that bhikkhu had a purpose for which he applied himself to painful striving, and that purpose has been achieved.
mn101:27.10: That is why, on a later occasion, he does not apply himself to painful striving again.
mn101:28.1: Suppose, bhikkhus, a fletcher were to heat and warm an arrow-shaft between two flames, making it straight and workable.
mn101:29.1: When, bhikkhus, the fletcher’s arrow-shaft has been heated and warmed between two flames, and made straight and workable, that fletcher does not again heat and warm the arrow-shaft between two flames and make it straight and workable on a later occasion.
mn101:29.3: Because, bhikkhus, he had a purpose for which he heated and warmed the arrow-shaft between two flames and made it straight and workable, and that purpose has been achieved.
mn101:29.4: That is why he does not again heat and warm the arrow-shaft between two flames and make it straight and workable on a later occasion.
mn101:29.5: So too, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu considers thus:
mn101:29.6: ‘When I dwell at ease, unwholesome things increase in me and wholesome things decline;
mn101:29.7: but when I apply myself to painful striving, unwholesome things decline in me and wholesome things increase.
mn101:29.8: Suppose I were to apply myself to painful striving?’
mn101:29.9: So he applies himself to painful striving.
mn101:29.10: When he applies himself to painful striving, unwholesome things decline in him and wholesome things increase.
mn101:29.11: On a later occasion he does not apply himself to painful striving again.
mn101:29.13: Because, bhikkhus, that bhikkhu had a purpose for which he applied himself to painful striving, and that purpose has been achieved.
mn101:29.14: That is why, on a later occasion, he does not apply himself to painful striving again.
mn101:29.15: In this way too, bhikkhus, exertion is fruitful, striving is fruitful.
mn101:30.1: Again, bhikkhus, here a Tathāgata arises in the world, an Arahant, fully enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, enlightened, blessed.
mn101:30.2: He declares this world with its gods, its Māras, and its Brahmās, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, with its rulers and its people, which he has himself realized by direct knowledge.
mn101:30.3: He teaches a Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, and he reveals a life divine that is utterly perfect and pure.
mn101:31.1: A householder or a householder’s child, or one reborn into some other family, hears that Dhamma.
mn101:31.2: Having heard the Dhamma, he acquires faith in the Tathāgata.
mn101:31.3: Possessing that faith, he considers thus:
mn101:31.4: ‘Household life is crowded and dusty; life gone forth is wide open.
mn101:31.5: It is not easy, while living in a house, to lead the life divine utterly perfect and utterly pure as a polished shell.
mn101:31.6: Suppose I were to shave off my hair and beard, put on the yellow robe, and go forth from the home life into homelessness?’
mn101:31.7: On a later occasion, abandoning a small or a large fortune, abandoning a small or a large circle of relatives, he shaves off his hair and beard, puts on the yellow robe, and goes forth from the home life into homelessness.
mn101:32.1: Being thus gone forth and possessing the bhikkhus’ training and way of life, abandoning killing living beings, he becomes one who abstains from killing living beings, with rod and weapon laid aside, gentle and kindly, he abides compassionate to all beings.
mn101:32.2: Abandoning taking what is not given, he becomes one who abstains from taking what is not given, taking (only) what is given, expecting (only) what is given, he abides pure in himself by not stealing.
mn101:32.3: Abandoning what is not the life divine, he becomes one who lives the life divine, who lives apart abstaining from vulgar lechery.
mn101:32.4: Abandoning false speech, he becomes one who abstains from false speech, he speaks truth, cleaves to truth, is trustworthy, reliable and undeceiving of the world.
mn101:32.5: Abandoning malicious speech, he becomes one who abstains from malicious speech: as one who is neither a repeater elsewhere of what is heard here for the purpose of causing division from these, nor a repeater to these of what is heard elsewhere for the purpose of causing division from those, who is thus a reuniter of the divided, a promoter of friendships, and enjoying concord, rejoicing in concord, delighting in concord, he becomes a speaker of words that promote concord.
mn101:32.6: Abandoning harsh speech, he becomes one who abstains from harsh speech: he becomes a speaker of such words as are innocent, pleasing to the ear and lovable, as go to the heart, are civil, desired of many, and dear to many.
mn101:32.7: Abandoning gossip, he becomes one who abstains from gossip: as one who tells in season what is true and beneficial and the Dhamma and Discipline, he becomes a speaker of timely words, worth recalling, reasoned, measured and connected with good.
mn101:32.8: He becomes one who abstains from injuring seeds and plants.
mn101:32.9: He becomes one who eats in only one part of the day, refusing (food) at night and late meals.
mn101:32.10: He becomes one who abstains from dancing, singing, music and theatrical shows.
mn101:32.11: He becomes one who abstains from wearing of garlands, smartening with scent and embellishment with unguents.
mn101:32.12: He becomes one who abstains from high and large couches.
mn101:32.13: He becomes one who abstains from accepting gold and silver.
mn101:32.14: He becomes one who abstains from accepting raw corn.
mn101:32.15: He becomes one who abstains from accepting raw meat.
mn101:32.16: He becomes one who abstains from accepting women and girls.
mn101:32.17: He becomes one who abstains from accepting bondswomen and bondsmen.
mn101:32.18: He becomes one who abstains from accepting sheep and goats.
mn101:32.19: He becomes one who abstains from accepting poultry and pigs.
mn101:32.20: He becomes one who abstains from accepting elephants, cattle, horses and mares.
mn101:32.21: He becomes one who abstains from accepting fields and lands.
mn101:32.22: He becomes one who abstains from going on errands.
mn101:32.23: He becomes one who abstains from buying and selling.
mn101:32.24: He becomes one who abstains from false weights, false metal and false measures.
mn101:32.25: He becomes one who abstains from cheating, deceiving, defrauding and trickery.
mn101:32.26: He becomes one who abstains from wounding, murdering, binding, brigandage, plunder and violence.
mn101:33.1: He becomes one who is content with robes to keep the body, with alms-food to keep the belly: wherever he goes he takes all with him.
mn101:33.2: Just as wherever a winged bird flies it flies using its own wings,
mn101:33.3: so too he becomes one who is content with robes to keep the body, with alms-food to keep the belly: wherever he goes he takes all with him.
mn101:33.4: Possessing this store of Noble Ones’ virtue, he feels in himself pleasure that is blameless.
mn101:34.1: He becomes one who, on seeing a visible form with the eye, apprehends no signs and features
mn101:34.2: through which, if he left the eye faculty unguarded, evil unprofitable dhammas of covetousness and grief might invade him. He practises the way of restraint, he guards the eye faculty, undertakes the restraint of the eye faculty.
mn101:34.3: On hearing a sound with the ear …
mn101:34.4: On smelling an odour with the nose …
mn101:34.5: On tasting a flavour with the tongue …
mn101:34.6: On touching a tangible with the body …
mn101:34.7: On cognizing a dhamma with the mind he apprehends no signs and features
mn101:34.8: through which, if he left the mind faculty unguarded, evil unprofitable dhammas of covetousness and grief might invade him. He practises the way of restraint, he guards the mind faculty, undertakes the restraint of the mind faculty.
mn101:34.9: Possessing this Noble Ones’ faculty restraint, he feels in himself pleasure that is unsullied.
mn101:35.1: He becomes one who acts in full awareness when moving forward and moving backward, who acts in full awareness when looking towards and looking away, who acts in full awareness when flexing and extending, who acts in full awareness when wearing the patched cloak, robes and bowl, who acts in full awareness when eating, drinking, chewing and tasting, who acts in full awareness when evacuating the bowels and making water, who acts in full awareness when walking, standing, sitting, waking up, talking and keeping silent.
mn101:36.1: Possessing this store of the Noble Ones’ virtue, and possessing this noble contentment, and possessing this Noble Ones’ faculty restraint, and possessing this Noble Ones’ mindfulness and full awareness,
mn101:36.2: he resorts to a secluded resting-place—to the forest, a tree-root, a rock, a ravine, a mountain cave, a charnel ground, a woodland solitude, an open space, a heap of straw.
mn101:36.3: On return from his alms-round after the meal, he sits down, folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, establishing mindfulness before him.
mn101:37.1: Abandoning covetousness for the world, he abides with a mind free from covetousness, he purifies mind from covetousness.
mn101:37.2: Abandoning ill-will and hatred, he abides without a mind of ill-will, compassionate for the welfare of all living beings, he purifies mind from ill-will and hatred.
mn101:37.3: Abandoning lethargy and drowsiness, he abides with a mind free from lethargy and drowsiness, percipient of light, mindful and fully aware, he purifies mind from lethargy and drowsiness.
mn101:37.4: Abandoning agitation and worry, he abides unagitated with a mind stilled in himself, he purifies mind from agitation and worry.
mn101:37.5: Abandoning uncertainty, he abides with a mind crossed beyond uncertainty, unquestioning about profitable dhammas, he purifies mind from uncertainty.
mn101:38.1: Having thus abandoned these five hindrances, imperfections of mind that weaken understanding,
mn101:38.2: quite secluded from sensual desires, secluded from unprofitable dhammas, he enters upon and abides in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by initial and sustained application, with happiness and pleasure born of seclusion.
mn101:38.3: In this way too, bhikkhus, exertion is fruitful, striving is fruitful.
mn101:39.1: Again, bhikkhus, with the stilling of initial and sustained application, a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the second jhāna, which has internal placidity and singleness of mind, without initial application, without sustained application, with joy and pleasure born of concentration.
mn101:39.2: In this way too, bhikkhus, exertion is fruitful, striving is fruitful.
mn101:40.1: Again, bhikkhus, with the fading away of joy as well, a bhikkhu dwells in equanimity, mindful and fully aware, and feels pleasure with the body; he enters upon and abides in the third jhāna, on account of which the noble ones announce: ‘He dwells happily who has equanimity and is mindful.’
mn101:40.2: In this way too, bhikkhus, exertion is fruitful, striving is fruitful.
mn101:41.1: Again, bhikkhus, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the fourth jhāna, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.
mn101:41.2: In this way too, bhikkhus, exertion is fruitful, striving is fruitful.
mn101:42.1: When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs it, inclines it, to the knowledge of recollection of past lives.
mn101:42.2: He recollects his manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many aeons of world-contraction, many aeons of world-expansion, many aeons of world-contraction and expansion: ‘there I was so named, of such a clan, with such an appearance, such was my food, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such my life-span; and passing away from there, I reappeared elsewhere; and there too I was so named, of such a clan, with such an appearance, such was my food, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such my life-span; and passing away from there, I reappeared here’—thus he recollects his manifold past lives with their aspects and particulars.
mn101:42.3: In this way too, bhikkhus, exertion is fruitful, striving is fruitful.
mn101:43.1: When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs it, inclines it, to the knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings.
mn101:43.2: With the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, he sees beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, fair and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate; he understands how beings pass on according to their actions: ‘these beings who were ill-conducted in body, speech, and mind, revilers of the noble ones, wrong in view, undertaking action based on wrong view, on the dissolution of the body, after death, have reappeared in a state of deprivation, in a bad destination, in perdition, even in hell; but these beings who were well-conducted in body, speech, and mind, not revilers of the noble ones, right in view, undertaking action based on right view, on the dissolution of the body, after death, have reappeared in a good destination, even in the heavenly world’—thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, he sees beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, fair and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate; he understands how beings pass on according to their actions.
mn101:43.3: In this way too, bhikkhus, exertion is fruitful, striving is fruitful.
mn101:44.1: When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs it, inclines it, to the knowledge of the exhaustion of the taints.
mn101:44.2: He understands as it actually is: ‘This is suffering’; he understands as it actually is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he understands as it actually is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he understands as it actually is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’;
mn101:44.3: he understands as it actually is: ‘These are the taints’; he understands as it actually is: ‘This is the origin of the taints’; he understands as it actually is: ‘This is the cessation of the taints’; he understands as it actually is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of the taints.’
mn101:45.1: Knowing and seeing thus, his mind is liberated from the taint of sensual desire, liberated from the taint of being, liberated from the taint of ignorance.
mn101:45.2: When it is liberated, there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated.’
mn101:45.3: He understands: ‘Birth is exhausted, the life divine has been lived, what was to be done is done, there is no more of this to come.’
mn101:45.4: In this way too, bhikkhus, exertion is fruitful, striving is fruitful.
mn101:46.1: This, bhikkhus, is the doctrine of the Tathāgatas.
mn101:46.2: For the Tathāgatas who hold this doctrine, bhikkhus, there are ten legitimate grounds for praise.
mn101:46.3: If, bhikkhus, beings experience pleasure and pain because of what was done in the past,
mn101:46.4: then surely, bhikkhus, the Tathāgata was a doer of good deeds in the past, since he now feels such taintless, pleasant feelings.
mn101:46.5: If, bhikkhus, beings experience pleasure and pain because of creation by a supreme god,
mn101:46.6: then surely, bhikkhus, the Tathāgata was created by a good supreme god, since he now feels such taintless, pleasant feelings.
mn101:46.7: If, bhikkhus, beings experience pleasure and pain because of circumstance,
mn101:46.8: then surely, bhikkhus, the Tathāgata has good circumstances, since he now feels such taintless, pleasant feelings.
mn101:46.9: If, bhikkhus, beings experience pleasure and pain because of class of origin,
mn101:46.10: then surely, bhikkhus, the Tathāgata has a good class of origin, since he now feels such taintless, pleasant feelings.
mn101:46.11: If, bhikkhus, beings experience pleasure and pain because of present exertion,
mn101:46.12: then surely, bhikkhus, the Tathāgata has made good present exertion, since he now feels such taintless, pleasant feelings.
mn101:46.13: If, bhikkhus, beings experience pleasure and pain because of what was done in the past, the Tathāgata is to be praised;
mn101:46.14: if beings do not experience pleasure and pain because of what was done in the past, the Tathāgata is to be praised.
mn101:46.15: If, bhikkhus, beings experience pleasure and pain because of creation by a supreme god, the Tathāgata is to be praised;
mn101:46.16: if beings do not experience pleasure and pain because of creation by a supreme god, the Tathāgata is to be praised.
mn101:46.17: If, bhikkhus, beings experience pleasure and pain because of circumstance, the Tathāgata is to be praised;
mn101:46.18: if beings do not experience pleasure and pain because of circumstance, the Tathāgata is to be praised.
mn101:46.19: If, bhikkhus, beings experience pleasure and pain because of class of origin, the Tathāgata is to be praised;
mn101:46.20: if beings do not experience pleasure and pain because of class of origin, the Tathāgata is to be praised.
mn101:46.21: If, bhikkhus, beings experience pleasure and pain because of present exertion, the Tathāgata is to be praised;
mn101:46.22: if beings do not experience pleasure and pain because of present exertion, the Tathāgata is to be praised.
mn101:46.23: This, bhikkhus, is the doctrine of the Tathāgatas.
mn101:46.24: For the Tathāgatas who hold this doctrine, bhikkhus, these ten legitimate grounds for praise apply.”
mn101:46.25: This is what the Blessed One said.
mn101:46.26: Those bhikkhus were satisfied and delighted in the Blessed One’s words.
